DESCRIPTION: How the books in Source Library describe four kinds of life: feeling alive, a living world, living made things, and places inhabited by spirits. {{points}} passages, each linked to its page.
DRAFTFLAG: Draft, 13 October 2026. The passages were found by searching the library’s English translations and were selected and checked by language models, as described under Method. No scholar has reviewed them yet. Every quotation is word for word from Source Library’s translation and links to its page, so each can be read in context and against the scan.
INTRO:
People have said that things are alive in at least four different senses, and the books in this library use all four.

  • Feeling alive. A person describes, from the inside, feeling alive or feeling dead: strength returning after illness, the world turning vivid, or the heaviness of acedia and melancholy.
  • The world as alive. A text says that something we would not call alive is alive: the cosmos has a soul, metals grow from seed, the stars are moved by souls, the earth breathes.
  • Made things as alive. A statue is filled with a god by a rite, a painting seems about to speak, a talisman holds a power for a set time. Christopher Alexander used the word “life” for a quality of buildings and towns, and his sense belongs here too.
  • The inhabited world. A river, a mountain, a tree or the soil is a person, or the home of one: a river god, a nymph of a spring, a nāga in a lake, a lord of the soil. People make offerings to them and can offend them. Anthropologists call this animism.

The map below places every passage found for each sense by when the work was written, or, with a switch, by the date of the edition the library holds. Below it, each sense is described with examples, followed by how common each one is, when its vocabulary rises and falls, and which traditions it comes from.
FINDINGS:
The four senses

1. Feeling alive

Passages that describe from the inside what it is like to feel alive are rare: {{confirmed.felt_alive}} were found, and {{confirmed.felt_dead}} that describe feeling dead inside. The searches for this sense retrieved {{felt_probes.retrieved}} passages; {{felt_probes.judged}} were read closely and {{felt_probes.confirmed_own}} confirmed. Most describe joy, grief, rapture or relief without describing the feeling as being alive. None of the {{baseline_n}} random pages describes it.

Swedenborg: “Consequently, all the perceptive and sensitive faculties seemed alive with happiness.” Petrarch, on his melancholy: “…a time not of light or life, but resembles a Tartarean night.”

2. The world as alive

This is the largest group: {{confirmed.world_alive}} passages. What is said to be alive is most often the cosmos as a whole ({{world_carriers.0.1}} passages), then metals and minerals ({{world_carriers.1.1}}), the heavens and stars ({{world_carriers.2.1}}), the earth ({{world_carriers.3.1}}) and plants ({{world_carriers.4.1}}). The life is credited to a soul or form ({{world_sources.0.1}}), to seed and growth ({{world_sources.1.1}}), to God ({{world_sources.2.1}}) or to a breath or spirit ({{world_sources.3.1}}). Ficino, translating Plato: “it must be said that this world is an animal, truly constituted by divine providence.” The Theatrum chemicum: “Since, therefore, metals grow and have a beginning, it also follows that they are multiplied.”

The opposite claim, that matter is dead, appears in the same period. Counting phrases across all translated pages, the vocabulary of growing metals runs at {{lexical.dims.living_minerals.rate.0}} occurrences per 10,000 pages in editions printed before 1400, {{lexical.dims.living_minerals.rate.3}} in the 1600s and {{lexical.dims.living_minerals.rate.5}} in the 1800s. Talk of a soul of the world peaks in the 1600s at {{lexical.dims.world_soul.rate.3}} and falls to {{lexical.dims.world_soul.rate.5}}. The vocabulary of dead matter (“brute matter”, “inert matter”, “automata”) stands at {{lexical.dims.dead_matter.rate.1}} in the 1400s and rises to {{lexical.dims.dead_matter.rate.3}} in the 1600s. Henry More, 1662: “Matter is inert, or destitute of vital sympathy and shared activity”. The argument also took place within alchemy. Michael Maier, 1618: “In metals, no nutrition, growth, or extension in all dimensions is found”. These counts describe the editions the library holds, dated by edition; they are not a measure of European thought as a whole. Dated by when the works were written instead, the passages calling matter dead are still late: {{work_eras.rows.world_dead.work.3}}% come from works of the 1600s and {{work_eras.rows.world_dead.work.4}}% from works written after 1700.

3. Made things as alive

{{confirmed.made_alive}} passages call a made thing alive. Most concern images and statues ({{made_carriers.0.1}}) or other crafted works ({{made_carriers.1.1}}), and the life comes from the maker’s skill ({{made_sources.0.1}}) or from a consecration ({{made_sources.1.1}}). The sentence quoted most often, in edition after edition and in Augustine’s City of God, comes from the Hermetic Asclepius: “I mean animated statues, full of sense and spirit, performing such great and such kinds of things.” A life given by a rite can also end. Gaffarel’s talisman, once its hour has passed, “remains void and useless, cold and dead.”

Alexander’s sense, the life of a place, a garden or a building, is almost absent. Searches for living places, gardens, buildings as bodies, wholeness and the spirit of a place retrieved {{alexander.retrieved}} passages, and {{alexander.confirmed}} were confirmed.
LEX_INTRO: These counts use no model. Each panel is one set of phrases, counted across every translated page in the library and divided by the number of translated pages from editions of that century. Green is the world, pink made things, blue the person; the dashed line is the vocabulary of dead matter.
RATES_INTRO: The random columns give the base rate: {{baseline_n}} pages drawn at random from the whole translated library and read by the same two passes. For the first three senses, the first pass flagged {{baseline_any.screened}} of them ({{baseline_any.screen_rate.0}}%); the second kept {{baseline_any.confirmed}}. The last column counts confirmed passages among those the searches retrieved, which depends on how many searches each sense had, so it is comparable only within a row.
QUAL_INTRO: Each passage was also tagged with the qualities it gives to the life it describes, from a fixed list of twenty that includes Alexander’s terms (wholeness, proportion, belonging, interiority). Each bar is the share of confirmed passages naming that quality.
MEET_INTRO: The four senses mostly appear in different books. Of the {{books}} books with a passage on the first three senses, {{books_by_layers.1}} have passages on one sense only, {{books_by_layers.2}} on two, and none on all three. Of the {{animism.books}} books with a passage on the inhabited world, {{animism.books_also_world_alive}} also say the world itself is alive. Each row of the table asks: among books with one kind of passage, how many also have another? A book enters this sample through the few passages a search found in it, so “without” means “not found here”, not “absent from the book”.
METHOD:
1. Search. For the first three senses, 25 dimensions, each with an opposite (feeling dead inside, matter as mechanism, lifeless work), searched two ways: 151 English phrases matched exactly in the English translations (133 found something), and four probe sentences per dimension matched by meaning against 4.54 million page embeddings. For the inhabited world, 69 English phrases in ten groups (spirits of place, waters, mountains, trees, animals, ancestors, dwelling, offerings and appeasement, the earth as kin, and named systems such as kami and manitou), with 60 pages drawn at random per phrase ({{animism.draw.retrieved}} in all).
  2. Screen. gemini-3.1-flash-lite marks each passage for each sense and must quote, word for word, the sentence that shows it. If the quotation is not on the page, the mark is dropped. The comparison ignores inline notes and markup, not words.
  3. Judge. Every passage the screen marked is read again by gemini-3.8-flash under a strict rubric: a mark stands only if a careful reader would agree the passage states it outright. Analogies, allegory, single emotion words and ordinary biology are rejected; reported doctrines (“Plato holds the world is an animal”) count. For the inhabited world, gods of heaven, angels, metaphor and the world soul are rejected, and the judge assigns the voice.
  4. Second reader. Claude (Opus), a different model family, read {{second_rater.n}} passages without seeing the judge’s verdicts: 20 the judge confirmed, 20 it rejected, 20 the screen passed over. It agreed with all 20 confirmations (agreement {{second_rater.agree}} of {{second_rater.n}}, Cohen’s kappa {{second_rater.kappa}}), would have accepted 4 of the rejections, and found 6 positives among the screen’s negatives. Those 6 showed that the quotation check was discarding true quotations over markup; the check was fixed and 550 passages were screened again. The counts here are therefore a lower bound.
  5. Base rate. The {{baseline_n}}-page random sample from the map of conscious experiences, read by the same passes for all four senses.
  6. Phrases and meaning. Exact phrases found far more of this material than meaning search. Of the passages the judge read, {{lanes.lexical.confirm_of_judged.0}}% of those found by phrase were confirmed, against {{lanes.embedding.confirm_of_judged.0}}% of those found by meaning (n = {{lanes.embedding.judged}}). The embedding space groups pages by book and language more than by idea.
  7. A cheaper ranker. Jev, a small decision model from a different maker, answered the inhabited-world rubric as a yes-or-no question on every page the screen read ({{animism.jev.scored}} pages, about $0.20). Its scores separate confirmed from unconfirmed passages at AUC {{animism.jev.auc_all}}; at a cut of 0.5 it keeps {{animism.jev.recall_at_half.0}}% of confirmed passages and flags {{animism.jev.flag_rate_baseline_at_half.0}}% of random pages. It can narrow a search across the whole library, but the counts on this page come from the judge.

All classification was done by models, on English translations. A passage that a translation softened or a model misread may be missing, and a passage on the map may be wrong. Each one links to its page so it can be checked.
DATA_NOTE: Every point on the map, with its quotation, book, date, language, sense, judge’s reason and page link, is in aliveness-data.json; every figure on this page is in aliveness-numbers.json. ANIM_INTRO:
Here a particular place or natural thing is treated as a person, or as the home of a person tied to that place. This differs from the world as alive: a nāga in a lake is a being who lives there, not a claim that water is alive. Each passage is also marked by who is speaking: the tradition’s own texts (insider), an observer describing other people’s beliefs (outsider: ethnographers, travellers, missionaries, critics), or a poet using a convention (literary).

How much there is

{{animism.confirmed.person}} passages were confirmed, from {{animism.books}} books in {{animism.languages}} edition languages. On a random page it is rare: {{animism.baseline.person.confirmed}} of {{animism.baseline_n}} random pages ({{animism.baseline.person.rate.0}}%, 95% interval {{animism.baseline.person.rate.1}}–{{animism.baseline.person.rate.2}}%), against {{baseline.world_alive.rate.0}}% for the world as alive. The first pass flagged {{animism.baseline.person.screened}} random pages that mention gods or spirits; the second found a spirit tied to a particular place on one of them.

These beings live in mountains and rocks ({{animism.dwelling.0.1}} passages), rivers, lakes and the sea ({{animism.dwelling.1.1}}), trees and forests ({{animism.dwelling.2.1}}) and the earth ({{animism.dwelling.3.1}}). Most are a deity of the place ({{animism.being.0.1}}) or a nature spirit ({{animism.being.1.1}}). What people do about them is, in order of frequency: worship them, make offerings, fear them, greet or address them, and appease them.

The Kanjur’s Vinaya, at the gates of Śrāvastī: “They made offerings to the local spirits, secured the gates, and waited.” A Chinese compendium: “When Liu Chong departed from the Western Capital and passed this mountain, the mountain barked loudly at him.” Virgil, in a 1583 edition, on Aeneas at his father’s tomb: “Uncertain whether he should think it the spirit of the place or the servant of his parent.”

Who speaks

Of {{animism.trad.tibetan_buddhist.person}} Tibetan Buddhist passages, {{animism.trad.tibetan_buddhist.insider}} come from the tradition’s own rites and narratives, in which nāgas, lords of the soil and mountain gods are addressed, given offerings and bound by oath. African, Native American and Pacific material is almost all reported by outsiders: {{animism.trad.african.outsider}} of {{animism.trad.african.person}} African passages, {{animism.trad.native_american.outsider}} of {{animism.trad.native_american.person}} Native American and {{animism.trad.pacific.outsider}} of {{animism.trad.pacific.person}} Pacific passages, mostly in 19th- and 20th-century ethnography written in English. Of all dated outsider passages, {{animism.voice_dated.outsider.share_from_1800}}% are in editions printed after 1800. E. B. Tylor, who gave the word “animism” its modern meaning, wrote in 1871: “In Siberia, the Yakuts worship the bear in common with the spirits of the forest, bowing toward his favorite haunts with appropriate phrases of prose and verse in praise of the bravery and generosity of their ‘beloved uncle.’” Greco-Roman passages are mostly literary ({{animism.trad.greco_roman.literary}} of {{animism.trad.greco_roman.person}}): nymphs and river gods in poetry. Chinese passages are divided among all three voices. These figures describe what the library holds, not the traditions themselves.

Passages that deny the belief are few: {{animism.confirmed.denied}}. Hegel, in 1837, on the Greek fountain nymph: “the meaning they attached to it was not an objective property of the fountain itself, but a subjective one”.
WHEN_INTRO:
A book in this library is usually a later edition of an older work: a 1532 printing of the Hermetic Asclepius, a 1583 Virgil, a 20th-century reprint of an 18th-century Tibetan woodblock. Of the {{work_dates.points}} passages on the map, {{work_dates.older_than_edition_100y}} come from works written at least a century before the edition they were read in. Placed by edition, almost nothing on the map is older than 1400. Placed by when the work was written, about a fifth of the passages on the world as alive and on the inhabited world, and a quarter of those on made things as alive, come from works written before 500 CE.

Each work date records what it rests on: a Wikidata record of the work, the author’s lifetime from Wikidata, a date printed on the title page, or a model’s estimate. The estimates were checked against 318 works with Wikidata dates, and 85% fell within the range given. Opening a passage shows its date and what it rests on.
